title: ML Architecture
lead: From a trained model to a maintainable, observable, governed system.
bullets: Software engineering for systems that depend on learned behavior.
One shared case: bank customer-churn prediction.
Two blocks: model-to-system foundations, then architecture and quality.
Five presenters: Ricardo, Tomás, Simon, Luca, and Matheus.
example: Bank churn supplies the shared case. Examples, records, schedules, and incidents are illustrative.
takeaway: A useful model needs an engineered system around it.

title: Two blocks, one shared bank case
lead: Follow the group’s topic outline; use the case to connect each architectural decision.
bullets: Block 1: lifecycle, serving, monitoring, and design decisions.
Block 2: tactics, MLOps, security, privacy, and quality.
Concept first: explain the mechanism, then apply it to churn.
Named handoffs: each section identifies its presenter; unassigned topics remain TBD.
example: The same source → feature → model → score → policy path returns throughout the lecture.
takeaway: Each architectural decision connects predictive behavior to a system responsibility.

title: The bank case: features, labels, and predictions
lead: A few ML terms connect familiar application data to a learned risk estimate.
bullets: Feature: a prepared input, such as logins during the previous seven days.
Label: the observed churn outcome used for training and later evaluation.
Prediction: an estimate produced before the customer’s future outcome is known.
Training vs. inference: learn from earlier examples; apply the approved model to current inputs.
example: Ana / C042: logins fall from 7 to 1; the illustrative score is 0.70. Her next-30-day outcome is unknown.
takeaway: Lower activity is evidence for a model input, not proof that a customer will leave.

title: From a trained model to an ML system
lead: Architecture connects learning, production data, operational controls, and business decisions.
bullets: Training uses historical features and labels to build and evaluate candidates.
Production validates current data and applies an approved, compatible model.
Stored scores link predictions to customer, time, input evidence, and versions.
Business policy determines the permitted action; it remains separate from the score.
example: The bank computes a monthly batch of churn scores, then applies campaign eligibility and contact rules.
takeaway: Keep the learning path and production path distinct, but traceable.

title: Two lifecycles, one compatible system
lead: Code correctness and predictive usefulness depend on different feedback and release cycles.
bullets: Software changes can be checked through code, contract, and integration tests.
Model development also needs representative data, suitable labels, and evaluation.
Feedback differs: execution checks may be immediate; churn labels arrive later.
Co-versioning links changes across code, feature meaning, model, and configuration.
example: A CRM connector can change today while M1 stays fixed; its changed inputs can still alter predictions.
takeaway: A passing software test does not establish future predictive quality.

title: Prediction and business action are separate
lead: A model estimates risk. Business rules decide whether and how the bank may act.
bullets: Score: estimated churn risk, not a guaranteed outcome.
Policy: preferences, eligibility, contact limits, and campaign budget.
Action: an offer, another response, or no contact at all.
Separate evaluation: predictive quality and the benefit of an offer are different questions.
example: Ana may have a high risk score and still receive no offer because contact preferences or policy prohibit it.
takeaway: A policy change should not require retraining the prediction model.
